Understanding Your Data

Taking the time to understand your data thoroughly is arguably the most important part of any analysis. Sometimes sources of confusion can arise from the data itself, especially when it contradicts existing knowledge.

Example
In an observational study, we were looking at the effects of two surgical interventions (A, B). The surgical interventions were applied across multiple rooms (1, 2, 3, 4). Hospital facilities experts in charge of environmental controls assured us that the rooms were identical in their ability to manage the environment. One thing that was known to fluctuate was humidity, which was affected by the outdoor humidity. When outdoor humidity rose, environmental controls responded by decreasing the humidity to keep humidity levels below a certain point. However when outdoor humidity fell, the room controls did not add humidity. Thus humidity was known to fall when it was dry outside. We thus made the decision to collect room humidity data.
In our initial analysis, we noticed that % humidity in room 4, specifically for intervention B had lower humidities compared to intervention A in the same room and both interventions across the other rooms (see figure below). This was a cause for concern since if the rooms were identical, why was the humidity for one room for one intervention noticeably different from the others? Further, this could have been a signal that the rooms were, in fact, not identical. Our initial response was that there may be some kind of relationship or interaction between intervention B and room 4 that ultimately caused a drop in humidity. We prepared to account for this in our final model, potentially including room number as a covariate.









But as we took the time to understand our data, we noticed that the lower humidity for room 4 and intervention B was not due to an interaction. Instead, it was a result of the chronology or seasonality of patient enrolment. Due to the passive nature of our enrolment method, enrolments for patients receiving intervention B in room 4 happened to be concentrated between January through March 2026 (see figure below). In the geographical region of this study, these were the winter months where humidity tended to be at a minimum. This resolved the conflict between our facilities experts and the data and saved us from introducing covariates that, in reality, did not explain variation which would have reduced the power of the analysis.

    About
    
      About Me
      My name is Ben Ouyang. For the past 20 years, I have worked at the intersection of epidemiology, statistics and comparative medicine to improve human and animal lives. This cross-functional experience has taught me how to use statistics to empower the non-statistical expert. My goal is to help you understand your dataset so that you can be confident in leaning on your own expertise to make the decisions you need to make. 
    
  




  
    Services
    
      What We Do
      
        
          Study Design
          For those undertaking a new investigation and would like help with things like formulation of research objectives/questions/hypotheses, protocols, selecting what data to collect, sample size calculations and database structure.
        
        
          Data cleaning, merging and formatting
          Sometimes data has been collected, but it's not quite ready for analysis. Human errors in data entry can cause incongruencies that make analysis difficult. Sometimes data comes from multiple sources and they need to be merged. And other times, data is in various formats that cannot coexist without compromising the integrity of your data. These issues are often the most challenging and time-consuming part of data work. I perform the complex operations needed to get your dataset in shape for your analysis while keeping a record of each operation to ensure reproducibility and repeatability.
        
        
          Understanding your data
          Often the most important part of data work. I have found that statistics is most empowering for both the statistical and non-statistical expert when they have a nuanced and rich understanding of their data. I explore the data thoroughly and explain intricate phenomenon and patterns using salient visualizations that support an intuitive understanding of the final statistical model. 
          
          Click here for an example.
        
        
          Statistical modeling
          Using your study objective, design, and data collection methods, I conduct comparisons and build models that help explain the contributions of variables of interest to your outcomes. When study objectives are more open-ended, I conduct exploratory analyses governed by the expertise of you and your team to produce potential hypotheses to explore further. I aim for transparent and intuitive analyses that explain and illustrate the final results while concurrently elucidating the strengths, limitations, potentials for bias and possible next steps.
        
        
          Proof-of-concept artificial intelligence & machine learning models
          If you would like to see if your data can power predictions and classifications, I build preliminary artificial intelligence and machine learning models to help you get started. I  engineer features and provide insight into their associative, predictive and causal links to the outcome.
        
        
          Reporting and manuscript support
          If you are planning to publish your research in a scientific journal, I  provide documentation of the methods used as well as the results of the analysis. I work with your subject-matter experts to provide discussion points that are both scientifically and statistically relevant and sound
        
        
          Statistical and epidemiological training for clinical research
          If you need some guidance in building or applying your statistical and epidemiological tools but would ultimately like to do it yourself, consider this option. Good option for veterinary/medical interns, residents and other trainees involved in clinical research.
